memory: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that seemed so far off when I was a freshman. It's surreal to be at this stage. It feels like just yesterday I was in an intro class learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basics of quantum computing. It's exciting to see how far I've come.My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it directly connects to real-world problem-solving. For example, how do we optimize pathfinding in large networks or find the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity? These kinds of problems are fascinating to me. In the class, we've been diving into dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great; she has a knack for explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll put up a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to at least approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas.Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is definitely an adventure. We have to collaborate with folks who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about what the final product should look like. But that's also the beauty of it, right? In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle everything from concurrency issues to node failures gracefully. It's nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we got that fixed and everything ran smoothly, it was this huge sense of accomplishment.I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. To be honest, I've always been a gamer at heart, so this was a must-take. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.I'm also taking an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which might have been intimidating at first, but I'm actually enjoying it now. The professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff that has made me rethink how I approach problems.I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it applies to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of discussions, which is a nice change of pace from the coding in my other classes. It's great to sit back and analyze abstract ideas. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was a fascinating experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.As for my schedule, I'm doing the typical college juggle. Mondays and Wednesdays are packed. I start at 9:30 am with Advanced Algorithms, then I have a short break to refuel before heading to my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be all over the place – sometimes it's a lecture, sometimes it's lab work, and sometimes it's project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with just Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be brutal if I'm tired from the rest of the day. But hey, it's senior year, and I have to push through. Fridays are open, with no scheduled classes, but inevitably, I'm working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab that's focusing on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload.The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and that's without considering any major bugs or model training issues. The Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a mini-nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of a real job environment. It's a great opportunity to apply everything I've learned so far.Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night – once in a while, you just can't avoid it, especially if something's due the next day and you're stuck debugging. However, it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. I guess the biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.I'm glad you're enjoying your hobbies! It's great that you find ways to balance your intense schedule with activities that bring you joy. Having a break from coding can definitely help you come back to it with a fresh perspective.
